Q: How do I calculate the percentage of ids with at least one record in a given group from a different table in SQL Server 2019? A:

You can break down the task into several steps:

  1. Count the distinct users that have accessed each application. This can be accomplished with a combination of COUNT(DISTINCT UserID) and GROUP BY AppName.
  2. Count the total number of users.
  3. Combine the two to calculate percentages.

One of several ways to write this query is:

SELECT
    UAC.AppName,
    UAC.UserAccessCount * 100.00 / UC.UserCount AS [% of users that have used app]
FROM (
    SELECT AAL.AppName, COUNT(DISTINCT AAL.UserID) AS UserAccessCount
    FROM AppAuditLog AAL
    GROUP BY AAL.AppName
) UAC
CROSS JOIN (
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS UserCount
    FROM Users
) UC
ORDER BY UAC.AppName

The above could also be rearranged to use CTEs (common table expressions):

WITH UserCount AS (
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS UserCount
    FROM Users
),
UserAccessCounts AS (
    SELECT AAL.AppName, COUNT(DISTINCT AAL.UserID) AS UserAccessCount
    FROM AppAuditLog AAL
    GROUP BY AAL.AppName
)
SELECT
    UAC.AppName,
    UAC.UserAccessCount * 100.00 / UC.UserCount AS [% of users that have used app]
FROM UserAccessCounts UAC
CROSS JOIN UserCount UC
ORDER BY UAC.AppName

Results:

AppName % of users that have used app
Analytics 75.0000000000000
Security 25.0000000000000
User Management 50.0000000000000

You can round or cast the result to achieve a specific desired precision. If you are running this query from an application, it is common (best?) practice just to leave the result as a simple fraction (0.75, etc.) and perform the scaling and rounding at the presentation layer. You would still need to cast the UserAccessCount value to a FLOAT, DECIMAL, or NUMERIC type before the divide to avoid integer division.

You can add date filters as needed, if you wish you report on accesses for specific time periods.

Note that this query will omit any apps that have no accesses. This can be fixed if you have a separate Apps table (which is why CharlieFace was asking in the comments). You could change the UserAccessCount part of the query to use a LEFT JOIN as follows:

    SELECT A.AppName, COUNT(DISTINCT AAL.UserID) AS UserAccessCount
    FROM Apps A
    LEFT JOIN AppAuditLog AAL
        ON AAL.AppName = A.AppName
    GROUP BY A.AppName

See this db<>fiddle for a demo.

Q: confuseing which one i take js or php for back end (laravel or node js ) A:

Things change. Realistically you're not going to have a whole career just using one language or framework anyway. Demand for developers familiar with different technologies will go up and down as fashion, economics, feature sets and a whole host of other factors change. New languages and frameworks will appear and some people will switch to those to get new capabilities, others will continue developing on their older (but perhaps better-understood and more stable) platforms. AI will also cannibalise a certain about of development work (maybe a lot, or far less, depending on how much of the current hype you buy into).

So rather than worrying about a specific language or framework very early on, the important thing is to ensure you have the foundational knowledge of core computer science / software engineering theory and principles. That way, you can easily re-train on anything when the need arises. You also need to ensure you work on the related skills - analysis, attention to detail, communication skills etc...which are the things that make a developer stand out (and which are hard for AI to replace).

The languages I learned when I started my programming journey are now either obsolete, unfashionable, or are still used but aren't something my current role requires. I've switched from Java to .NET; I've learned VBA, forgot it all, and then re-learned it again later; I've used JavaScript, PHP, Perl, Haskell, QuickBASIC, C++, Assembler, HTML, CSS and various other things at different times and for different needs. This was made easier by that deeper understanding - a lot of the same principles are applicable to almost any language and environment - even to so-called "low code" platforms.

All that aside, about the only thing that could objectively tip you in favour of JavaScript in the comparison above is that it's also used on the front-end - so to use React you'd first need to know JS at least to a basic level, and then of course nodeJS also uses JavaScript so you can use JS on the backend too. But then again if you're doing Laravel you'll probably still want some JS for your site's frontend anyway...so why not just learn both? Then you can add on React- and Node-specific stuff when your core JS knowledge is up to scratch.

Q: Logstash error : Failed to publish events caused by: write tcp YY.YY.YY.YY:40912->XX.XX.XX.XX:5044: write: connection reset by peer A:

I had the same problem. Starting filebeat as a sudo user worked for me.

sudo ./filebeat -e

I have made some changes to input plugin config, as specifying ssl => false but did not worked without starting filebeat as a sudo privileged user or as root.

In order to start filebeat as a sudo user, filebeat.yml file must be owned by root. Change whole filebeat folder permission to a sudo privileged user by using sudo chown -R sime_sudo_user:some_group filebeat-7.15.0-linux-x86_64/ and then chown root filebeat.yml will change the permission of file.
